newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Evans cautious on fiscal tightening.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Evans cautious on fiscal tightening.

text.p: Australian Treasury Secretary Ted Evans said on Thursday that it was not clear there was a case for tighter fiscal policy, particularly with high unemployment.
Evans said the government's 1997/98 budget which reduced the underlying budget deficit and continued the strategy begun in the 1996/97 budget kept the focus on the medium term.

"While there will always be a case for greater fiscal consolidation, it is not clear that there is a case for further accelerating consolidation, particularly with unemployment as high as it is," Evans said in a speech to business economists.

"Thus it was sensible to retrieve the slippage identified in the January 1997 mid-year review in 1998/99, rather than in 1997/98 when substantial fiscal consolidation measures announced in last year's budget are still to come into effect," he said.

Evans said the budget's medium term focus was an attempt to minimise over-reaction to short term fluctuations and to address those issues which might help ensure that the cycle is prolonged well into the medium term.
Experience showed that the fiscal consolidation in prospect within the government's projection period, to 2000/01 (June 30) would be needed as a buffer against cyclical developments.

"For this and other reasons, there is thus a premium on our prolonging the cycle -- on avoiding extremes, either in policy application or in outcomes," he said. "The medium term focus of macro-economic policies is driven by that objective."
In its 1997/98 budget, the government forecast an underlying budget deficit of A$3.9 billion for the year to June 30, 1998, compared with a estimated deficit of A$6.9 billion in 1996/97.
The government forecast an underlying surplus of A$1.60 billion for 1998/99 and an A$5.4 billion surplus in 1999/00.

The 1997/98 budget has been criticised by some in the business community as a missed opportunity, as it contained no policy surprises. "One favourable implicaiton of this medium term focus of fiscal policy is that there should be fewer surprises in each annual budget," Evans said.
"It is thus a little ironic that so many commentators and analysts appear to have been surprised by the absence of surprises in this budget," Evans said.
He also noted the budget's references to the role of structural reform in lifting the limits of growth, and thus reducing unemployment and inequality.

"In particular, it highlights the importance and interrelation of competition, productivity and competitiveness; and makes the simple but crucial point that while lack of competitiveness will stifle growth, achieving competitivness, in a global environment, will reduce demand side constraints -
leaving growth constrained only by a factor availability; the Asian experience if we are interested," he said.
"Are there limits to this process? In the medium term, no.

"In the short term, the persistence of structural rigidities in one area will limit the benefits of reform elsewhere," he sadi. "This explains the observed superior performance of comprehensive reform approaches," he added.

"Equally, it explains why there are benefits in persisting with reforms in areas with economy-wide effects; labour markets, tax systems, competition policy, communications and transportation," he said.
